title: Cellular respiration
note: Glucose is oxidized in stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, then oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane. NADH and FADH2 carry electrons to the electron transport chain, which builds an H+ gradient that ATP synthase uses to make most of the ATP.

read.title: Following the electrons
text: Cellular respiration is easiest to understand by following electrons. Glucose holds them in high-energy C–H bonds. Step by step, enzymes strip them away and hand them to carriers, mainly NAD+, which becomes NADH.

Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, netting two ATP and two NADH. Each pyruvate then enters a mitochondrion, loses a carbon as CO2, and becomes acetyl CoA, producing another NADH. In the citric acid cycle, acetyl CoA joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, and the cycle releases the remaining carbons as CO2 while loading more NADH and FADH2.

Up to this point the cell has made only a few ATP. The real payoff comes at the inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH2 deliver their electrons to the electron transport chain. As electrons pass from protein to protein, their energy pumps hydrogen ions into the intermembrane space. At the end of the chain, oxygen accepts the spent electrons and combines with H+ to form water.

The crowded hydrogen ions return to the matrix mainly through ATP synthase. Their flow spins part of the enzyme, which joins ADP and phosphate. This chemiosmosis makes about 90 percent of the ATP from aerobic respiration. Without oxygen, the chain backs up, and many cells fall back on fermentation.
